human: Julius Perceiver’s connected ideas: inheritance, attraction, relationships, ambition, social incentives, and physical reality. Select a topic to follow its explanation and source videos.
inheritance: Inherited dispositions contribute to appearance, temperament, and interests. Genetic recombination helps explain why siblings differ.
heritability: Heritability concerns differences within a population under particular conditions. Twin comparisons help examine inherited similarities across different upbringings.
environment: Interests and behavior help select and create surroundings. Knowing a predisposition can then change the conditions in which it operates.
preselection: Other women’s apparent interest supplies information about a man’s desirability. Availability and visible rival cues communicate alternatives.
care: Care and logistical attraction help sustain a desired relationship, especially when partners are close in perceived desirability.
attachment: An existing bond is considered as one possible explanation in the Austin Dunham anecdote. The video also considers a particular preference and leaves the choice open.
commitment: The personal stories connect desire with different aims: casual contact, commitment, a stable household, and choosing a mother for one’s children.
purpose: Generational replication extends continuity beyond one child to descendants and the community that helps them survive and reproduce.
incentives: What another person stands to gain can supply a stronger reason to act than gratitude for past service alone.
media: Viewing choices shape the feed; the feed then offers more of what holds attention. Familiar interests can reappear after an account reset.
ai: Julius’s 2026 position separates useful, revolutionary AI from claims of present AGI and the investment narrative surrounding it.
causation: The free-will argument traces a decision through wants, memories, inherited dispositions, and circumstances that the person did not originally choose.
agency: Clicking a video supplies the example: did you choose the desire to click, or the title, free time, memories, and dispositions that helped produce it?
recurrence: The proposed recurrence combines heat death, rare fluctuations, infinite duration, and determinism to argue for a repetition of cosmic history.
twins: Separated identical twins are a central illustration in the argument that inherited dispositions shape later similarity despite different upbringings.
populations: The island and country comparisons extend the inheritance argument from individuals to communities. The research notes treat the population-inference questions separately.
nutrition: A generation’s shared baseline and differences in rank among peers are separate questions. Better shared conditions can change the former without erasing the latter.
intervention: The snack-cabinet example uses knowledge of a predisposition to change what is available at home rather than rely only on willpower.
archetype-labels: Chad and Stacy name idealized highly attractive men and women; Becky describes a woman below the Stacy ideal. Discrepancy theory compares the alternatives within a relationship.
alternatives: Discrepancy theory links a larger perceived desirability gap with credible alternatives and stronger desire.
security: Uncertainty can increase the urgency of securing a desired partner. Too little care can also make that partner leave while desire persists.
dissatisfaction: Desire and dissatisfaction can coexist. A person can still want a partner and decide that the relationship is too insecure to continue.
reciprocity: Tit-for-tat begins with cooperation, returns cooperation, and responds when the other person cheats.
jealousy: A headband left on the table makes the possibility of another woman visible. The rival cue is intended to change perceived alternatives.
ghosting: Boyfriend baiting uses withdrawal to press a desired partner toward commitment. Monica’s commitment dispute supplies the recurring example.
agreements: Exclusivity changes what continued involvement means. Julius’s overlapping relationships with Gianna and Bella make those commitments concrete.
exit: Julius recommends leaving after discovered infidelity and seeking a relationship congruent with the individual.
esg: Ratings can affect access to capital, giving companies a financial reason to pursue a public position independently of personal convictions.
narratives: The customer-support example compares a modest productivity tool with a civilization-changing AGI story that can attract much more attention and funding.
feeds: Your choices about what to stop and watch begin changing a reset or borrowed account’s recommendations.
capability: Pattern recognition, tool use, general intelligence, and a profitable business are distinct capabilities and outcomes.
valuation: The 2026 argument is that revolutionary technology can coexist with inflated prices, as in the railroad and internet comparisons.
determinism: Physical determinism holds that earlier states and physical laws fix what follows. Laplace’s imagined intelligence knows every force and position.
compatibilism: The video asks whether you chose to want something, or instead inherited and encountered the variables that produced the want.
light-travel: The Mars illustration challenges the everyday sense of a shared distant present. The research notes discuss signal delay and simultaneity.
responsibility: The poisoned-drink thought experiment asks how consequences should differ when someone did not choose the cause of harmful conduct, and when the danger persists.
boltzmann: The short describes a hypothetical fluctuation-generated observer with apparent memories and contrasts it with a computer simulation built by a civilization.
mismatch: The snack example connects a formerly useful inclination to store energy with readily available food in a changed environment.
identity: Would recreating your physical state restore your consciousness, or produce an identical copy convinced of being you?
